summary: Defines a metric for the one-way delay of packets across Internet paths. It was replaced by RFC 7679.

plainLanguage.summary: This RFC defines how to measure the time a packet takes to travel in one direction across a network, and how to report that number so that different laboratories get comparable results. It also explains how much of the result comes from clock errors, and how to correct for them.

questions: why measure one-way delay instead of round trip
what is poisson sampling in network measurement
how is one way delay calibrated
subtitle: How to measure the time a packet takes to travel one way, and how to report that number so two labs agree.

tldr.problem: Network researchers need to know how long a packet takes to cross a path, and they need the number to mean the same thing in every laboratory that reports it.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC defines a singleton metric for a single packet, a sample metric that takes measurements at times drawn from a Poisson process, and four statistics over that sample. It also defines the clock, wire-time and calibration errors that the reported value must account for.
tldr.outcome: Two independent implementations can compare their measurements because the metric, its parameters, the error accounting and the reporting requirements are all fixed. The document has been replaced by RFC 7679.

today: RFC 2679 was a Proposed Standard published in September 1999. It has been obsoleted by RFC 7679, which is the current definition of the one-way delay metric for IPPM.

sections.title: Why Measure One-way Delay
sections.content:
One-way delay of a Type-P packet from a source host to a destination host is useful for several reasons. Some applications do not perform well, or at all, if the end-to-end delay between hosts is large relative to some threshold value. Erratic variation in delay makes it difficult or impossible to support many real-time applications. The larger the delay, the more difficult it is for transport-layer protocols to sustain high bandwidths.

The minimum value of the metric indicates the delay due only to propagation and transmission delay. It also indicates the delay that will likely be experienced when the path is lightly loaded, while values above the minimum indicate the congestion present in the path.

The RFC measures one-way delay rather than round-trip delay for four reasons. The path from a source to a destination may differ from the path back, so a round-trip measurement actually measures two distinct paths together. Even when the two paths are symmetric, they may have radically different performance characteristics because of asymmetric queueing. An application may depend mostly on performance in one direction: a file transfer using TCP may depend more on the direction the data flows than on the direction the acknowledgements travel. And in quality-of-service networks, provisioning in one direction may be radically different from the reverse, so the guarantees differ.
sections.plainLanguage: A one-way delay tells you how long a packet takes to reach the far end. A round-trip delay hides both directions in one number, and the two directions of a path are often not the same.

sections.title: Four Notions of Clock Uncertainty
sections.content:
Whenever a time is mentioned, it is measured in seconds and fractions of a second relative to UTC. The Framework document distinguishes four related notions of clock uncertainty, and the RFC uses all four to work out how much a delay measurement can be trusted.

Synchronization measures the extent to which two clocks agree on what time it is: the clock on one host might be 5.4 msec ahead of the clock on a second host. Accuracy measures the extent to which a given clock agrees with UTC: a clock might be 27.1 msec behind UTC. Resolution measures the precision of a given clock: an old Unix host whose clock ticks only once every 10 msec has a resolution of only 10 msec. Skew measures the change of accuracy, or of synchronization, with time: a clock gaining 1.3 msec per hour is 27.1 msec behind UTC at one time and only 25.8 msec an hour later.

The RFC notes that the terminology differs from the ITU-T documents, which come from a telephony background, while these definitions come from a computer systems background. The authors provide a rough mapping: synchronization and accuracy correspond to time error, resolution to the sampling period, and skew to time drift.
sections.plainLanguage: Two clocks can differ in four ways: they can disagree about the time, they can be off from UTC, they can be too coarse to record a moment precisely, and they can drift apart over time. Each one adds error to a delay measurement.

sections.title: The Singleton Metric
sections.content:
The singleton metric is named Type-P-One-way-Delay. Its parameters are Src, the IP address of a host, Dst, the IP address of a host, and T, a time. Its value is either a real number or an undefined, informally infinite, number of seconds.

The definition is precise. The Type-P-One-way-Delay from Src to Dst at T is dT means that Src sent the first bit of a Type-P packet to Dst at wire-time T and that Dst received the last bit of that packet at wire-time T+dT. The delay is undefined, informally infinite, when Src sent the first bit of a Type-P packet to Dst at wire-time T and Dst did not receive that packet.

The RFC discusses several issues that come up in practice. Real delay values are positive, so reporting a negative value as a real delay makes no sense, though an individual zero or negative value may still be useful when looking for the shape of a distribution. Since delay values will often be as low as the 100 usec to 10 msec range, Src and Dst have to be synchronized very closely: GPS systems afford synchronization to within several tens of usec, while ordinary NTP may allow synchronization to within several msec, depending on the stability and symmetry of the delay properties among the NTP agents used. A methodology also has to say whether a delay is infinite or merely very large, and simple upper bounds such as the 255 seconds theoretical upper bound on the lifetimes of IP packets can be used. If a packet is duplicated so that multiple non-corrupt copies arrive, the packet is counted as received and the first copy to arrive sets the delay. If a packet is fragmented and reassembly does not occur, the packet is deemed lost.
sections.plainLanguage: The metric is one number for one packet: the time between the sender putting the first bit on the wire and the receiver getting the last bit. If the packet never arrives, the number is infinite rather than missing.

sections.title: Measuring and Calibrating
sections.content:
The detailed methodology depends on the Type-P, which covers the protocol number, the UDP or TCP port number, the size, and the precedence. For a given Type-P the methodology proceeds as follows. Arrange that Src and Dst are synchronized, so that their clocks are very closely synchronized with each other and each fairly close to the actual time. At Src, select the Src and Dst IP addresses and form a test packet of Type-P with those addresses, filling any padding needed to reach a given size with randomized bits so that compression along the path does not make the delay look lower than it is. At Dst, arrange to receive the packet. At Src, place a timestamp in the prepared packet and send it. If the packet arrives within a reasonable period, take a timestamp as soon as possible on receipt and subtract the two timestamps to get an estimate of the one-way delay. If the packet fails to arrive within a reasonable period, the delay is undefined.

The error analysis must account for the clock uncertainty and for the difference between wire time and host time. A naive computation of Tdest minus Tsource is off by Tsynch plus or minus Rsource plus Rdest, so the clock-related problems introduce a total uncertainty of Esynch(t) plus Rsource plus Rdest. Software on the hosts can only measure host times, so the difference between wire time and host time adds a further uncertainty of Hsource plus Hdest.

Calibration is described as a decomposition: the measured value equals the true value plus a systematic error plus a random error. If the systematic error can be determined it can be compensated for in the reported results. At a minimum, a bound should be found such that the reported value is within the true value plus or minus that bound at least 95 percent of the time. Reasonable bounds on the clock-related and host-related uncertainties should be possible by careful design and by calibrating the instruments on a known, isolated network in a lab: a GPS time source shrinks the clock-related uncertainty, and connecting two instruments back to back with a high-speed serial link or isolated LAN segment bounds the host-related uncertainty, because the repeated measurements then measure the same one-way delay.
sections.plainLanguage: To measure the delay, both hosts need clocks that agree closely, and the sender timestamps the packet while the receiver timestamps its arrival. The difference between the two timestamps is the delay, plus whatever error the clocks contributed.

sections.title: The Poisson Sample and Its Statistics
sections.content:
The sample metric is named Type-P-One-way-Delay-Poisson-Stream. Its parameters are Src, Dst, T0 a time, Tf a time, and lambda, a rate in reciprocal seconds. Its units are a sequence of pairs, each pair holding a time T and a dT that is either a real number or an undefined number of seconds, with the values of T increasing monotonically.

To build the sample, compute a pseudo-random Poisson process beginning at or before T0 with average arrival rate lambda and ending at or after Tf, then select the time values greater than or equal to T0 and less than or equal to Tf. At each of those times, take the value of Type-P-One-way-Delay. The sample is the resulting sequence of time and delay pairs. If there are no pairs, the sequence has length zero and the sample is empty. The RFC does not constrain lambda except at the extremes: too large and the measurement traffic perturbs the network and causes congestion, too small and interesting network behaviour may be missed. The Poisson process is used to schedule the measurements; the test packets will generally not arrive at Dst according to a Poisson distribution, since they are influenced by the network.

Four statistics are defined over the sample, and in all of them undefined values are treated as infinitely large. The percentile is the Xth percentile of all the dT values, undefined if the sample is empty. The median is the median of all the dT values, and it differs from the 50th percentile only when the sample holds an even number of values, in which case the mean of the two central values is used. The minimum is the smallest dT value, and it is undefined if every value is undefined. The inverse percentile is the fraction of all the dT values less than or equal to a given time duration threshold, and it could be as low as 0 percent or as high as 100 percent.
sections.plainLanguage: A sample is a series of delay measurements taken at times drawn at random from a Poisson process, which keeps the measurement times from falling into a pattern. Four numbers summarize it: a percentile, a median, a minimum and the share of measurements below a given threshold.

sections.title: Security and Privacy
sections.content:
Conducting Internet measurements raises both security and privacy concerns. The memo does not specify an implementation of the metrics, so it does not directly affect the security of the Internet or of applications running on it, but implementations of the metrics must be mindful of both concerns.

There are two types of security concern: potential harm caused by the measurements, and potential harm to the measurements. The measurements could cause harm because they are active and inject packets into the network. The measurement parameters MUST be carefully selected so that the measurements inject trivial amounts of additional traffic into the networks they measure. If they inject too much traffic they can skew the results of the measurement, and in extreme cases cause congestion and denial of service.

The measurements themselves could be harmed by routers giving measurement traffic a different priority than normal traffic, or by an attacker injecting artificial measurement traffic. If routers can recognize measurement traffic and treat it separately, the measurements will not reflect actual user traffic. If an attacker injects artificial traffic that is accepted as legitimate, the loss rate will be artificially lowered. The measurement methodologies SHOULD therefore include techniques to reduce the probability that measurement traffic can be distinguished from normal traffic, and authentication techniques such as digital signatures may be used where appropriate to guard against injected traffic attacks. The privacy concerns of network measurement are limited by the active measurements described here: unlike passive measurements, there can be no release of existing user data.
sections.plainLanguage: Measuring delay means sending real packets into the network, so the measurements must be light enough not to disturb the path being measured. And the packets must look like ordinary traffic, or the numbers will not reflect what real users see.

viz.caption: FOUR WAYS TWO CLOCKS CAN DISAGREE

items.title: Synchronization
items.text: How far apart two clocks are: one host's clock might be 5.4 msec ahead of another's.

items.title: Accuracy
items.text: How far a single clock is from UTC: a clock might be 27.1 msec behind it.

items.title: Resolution
items.text: How precisely a clock marks a moment: a clock ticking every 10 msec has a 10 msec resolution.

items.title: Skew
items.text: How the error changes over time: a clock gaining 1.3 msec per hour drifts.
